contagious: Many viral and bacterial infections are contagious. Avoid close contact, wash hands frequently, and do not share utensils until you have been fever-free for 24 hours.
duration: Common viral illnesses typically resolve in 5-10 days. Bacterial infections may lead to longer symptoms and may require clinical treatment if they persist beyond a week.
how long: Duration varies. Colds and flu usually last a week. If symptoms worsen after day 5, please consider a follow-up consultation with one of our specialists.
medicine: Only take medications as prescribed. Over-the-counter options like acetaminophen can manage fever, while ibuprofen can reduce inflammation. Consult your doctor first.
medication: Always verify dosages with a professional. Avoid combining multiple medications with the same active ingredients (e.g., cold medicine and pain relievers).
diet: Focus on the BRAT diet (Banana, Rice, Applesauce, Toast) for gastrointestinal issues. For general recovery, lean proteins and steamed vegetables are excellent.
exercise: Rest is therapeutic. Avoid high-intensity workouts during acute illness. Gentle movement like stretching or a 10-minute walk is usually safe if you are fever-free.
emergency: GO TO THE ER IMMEDIATELY for: Chest pain, sudden shortness of breath, severe allergic reactions, uncontrollable bleeding, or loss of consciousness.
severe: Any symptom that prevents you from eating, drinking, or sleeping should be professionally evaluated within 24 hours.
hydration: Aim for 2-3 liters of water daily. If you are losing fluids through fever or stomach issues, use oral rehydration salts (ORS).
sleep: Sleep is the body's primary healing mechanism. Ensure 7-9 hours in a cool, dark room. Elevate your head if you have nasal congestion.
vitamin c: Vitamin C is essential for immune cell function. While it won't 'cure' a cold, it may shorten the duration. Found in bell peppers, oranges, and strawberries.
vitamin d: Vitamin D plays a critical role in immune health. Many people are deficient; check your levels with a doctor and consider a supplement during winter months.
zinc: Zinc can help block viral replication if taken early. Use caution as high doses can cause nausea and interfere with other mineral absorption.
honey: Honey is a natural cough suppressant and antimicrobial. One teaspoon before bed is often more effective than standard cough syrups for soothing throats.
ginger: Ginger is excellent for calming nausea and reducing inflammation. Brew fresh ginger tea with lemon for the best natural relief.
turmeric: Turmeric contains curcumin, a potent anti-inflammatory. It is best absorbed when taken with a pinch of black pepper.
gargle: Gargling with warm salt water (1/2 tsp salt in 1 cup water) helps draw out excess fluid from inflamed throat tissues and reduces pain.
steam: Inhaling steam from a bowl of hot water or a warm shower helps loosen mucus in your sinuses and lungs.
humidifier: A humidifier adds moisture to the air, which prevents your nasal passages and throat from becoming painfully dry during the night.
alcohol: Avoid alcohol while sick. It dehydrates you, disrupts sleep quality, and can have dangerous interactions with many common medications.
smoking: Smoking significantly slows down respiratory healing and increases the risk of bronchitis and pneumonia during a cold or flu.
caffeine: Limit caffeine to 1 cup daily. It is a diuretic and can lead to dehydration and jitters when your body needs rest.
iron: Iron deficiency can cause extreme fatigue. If you are feeling chronically low on energy, ask your doctor to check your ferritin levels.
magnesium: Magnesium helps relax muscles and improve sleep quality. Found in spinach, almonds, and dark chocolate.
calcium: Calcium is vital for bone health and nerve transmission. Ensure adequate intake through dairy, fortified milks, or leafy greens.
omega-3: Omega-3 fatty acids found in fish oil help reduce systemic inflammation and support heart and brain health.
probiotic: Probiotics help restore healthy gut bacteria, especially important if you are on antibiotics or have digestive issues.
fever reduction: Cool down naturally with light clothing, a lukewarm sponge bath, and staying in a ventilated room. Avoid ice-cold baths as they cause shivering.
thermometer: For accurate oral readings, place the tip under your tongue for at least 60 seconds. Do not drink hot/cold fluids 20 minutes before testing.
bp cuff: Rest for 5 minutes before taking a blood pressure reading. Sit upright with feet flat on the floor and your arm at heart level.
inhaler: Always use a spacer if provided for your inhaler. Rinse your mouth after using steroid inhalers to prevent oral thrush.
glucometer: Wash your hands with soap before testing. Alcohol swabs can sometimes interfere with readings; soap and water is preferred.
pulse oximeter: Ensure your finger is warm and free of nail polish for the most accurate oxygen saturation (SpO2) reading.
mask: A N95 or KN95 mask is the most effective way to prevent spreading or catching respiratory pathogens in crowded areas.
hand washing: Scrub with soap for at least 20 seconds, especially after blowing your nose, using the restroom, or before eating.
sanitizer: Use hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol when soap and water are unavailable. Rub until your hands are completely dry.
disinfectant: Clean high-touch surfaces like doorknoobs, phones, and light switches daily to prevent the spread of germs in your home.
sun exposure: Some medications cause photosensitivity. If you are on antibiotics, wear SPF 50 and avoid direct sunlight to prevent severe burns.
driving: Do not drive if you have had a fever in the last 24 hours or if your medications cause drowsiness or blurred vision.
air travel: If you have an ear infection, talk to a doctor before flying. Pressure changes can cause severe pain or eardrum damage.
pets: Avoid letting pets lick your face or sharing your bedding while you are acutely ill to prevent cross-contamination of bacteria.
work: Returning to work too early slows your recovery and risks infecting colleagues. Stay home until you are fever-free without medication.
sick leave: A medical certificate can be issued by our clinicians to support your recovery at home. Prioritize your health over your schedule.
school: Children should stay home from school if they have a fever, persistent cough, or undiagnosed rash to protect the classroom.
pregnancy: Consult your OBGYN before taking ANY medications. Paracetamol is generally safe, but NSAIDs like ibuprofen are usually avoided.
loneliness: Isolation during illness is hard. Video call a friend or family member; social connection is proven to lower cortisol and aid healing.
anxiety: Feeling anxious about your health is normal. Practice box breathing: Inhale for 4, hold for 4, exhale for 4, hold for 4.
stress: Stress sends signals to the immune system to 'stand down.' Prioritize relaxation, soft music, and limited screen time.
reading: Reading is a great way to pass time during recovery, but avoid it if you have a fever or a migraine as it can cause eye strain.
tv: Limit TV or high-action movies if you have a headache. Low-volume podcasts or audiobooks are much gentler on the brain.
light: Photophobia (light sensitivity) is common with migraines and fevers. Keep your room dimly lit and wear sunglasses if needed.
noise: Excessive noise can increase blood pressure and heart rate. Maintain a quiet environment to allow your nervous system to rest.
garlic: Garlic has natural antimicrobial properties called Allicin. Eating it raw or lightly cooked can support respiratory health.
onion: Onions are rich in quercetin, a flavonoid that helps stabilize mast cells and reduce allergic responses.
citrus: Oranges and lemons provide hydration and Vitamin C, which help clear mucus and support collagen production for tissue repair.
leafy greens: Spinach and kale provide Vitamin K and Iron, essential for maintaining healthy blood and energy levels during recovery.
protein: High protein intake (eggs, chicken, tofu) provides the amino acids necessary to build the antibodies used to fight infection.
broth: Warm broth provides hydration and electrolytes (sodium/potassium) while being extremely gentle on an upset stomach.
soup: Chicken soup has a mild anti-inflammatory effect and the steam helps clear nasal passages. It is the ultimate recovery food.
ice: Ice is best for acute injuries like sprains. Apply for 15 minutes every 2-3 hours to reduce swelling and numb pain.
heat: Heat is better for chronic muscle stiffness or menstrual cramps. Use a heating pad on a low setting for 20 minutes.
message: Light massage can improve circulation but should be avoided over the direct site of an acute injury or if you have a fever.
elevation: If you have an injury or swelling in your legs, keep them raised above heart level to assist drainage and reduce pain.
burn: For minor burns, run cool (not cold) water over the site for 10 minutes. Do not use butter or oils as they trap heat.
cut: Clean cuts with mild soap and water. Apply pressure until bleeding stops, then use a sterile bandage.
scrape: Scrapes should be kept clean and moist. A thin layer of petroleum jelly and a bandage prevents painful scabbing.
bruise: Bruises change colors as they heal. If a bruise is accompanied by extreme swelling or if it appears without injury, seek care.
stitches: Keep stitches dry for the first 24-48 hours. Follow your doctor's instructions for cleaning to prevent scarring and infection.
bleeding: If a wound saturates a bandage in under 5 minutes, seek emergency medical attention immediately as it may require cautery.
aspirin: NEVER give aspirin to children as it carries a risk of Reye’s syndrome. Use pediatric-approved acetaminophen instead.
advil: Advil (ibuprofen) is excellent for reducing inflammation but should be taken with food to protect your stomach lining.
tylenol: Tylenol (acetaminophen) is the gold standard for fever reduction but must be used carefully to avoid liver toxicity.
laxative: Avoid overuse of laxatives. Increase fiber and water intake naturally first. Consult a doctor for persistent constipation.
antacid: Antacids neutralize stomach acid quickly but can interfere with the absorption of other medications if taken at the same time.
yoga: Restorative yoga helps lower heart rate and reduce pain perception. Focus on 'Child's Pose' for relaxation.
meditation: 5 minutes of daily meditation increases the production of 'natural killer' cells that find and destroy viruses.
hydration log: Keep a log of your water intake. Check your urine color; it should be pale yellow. Dark urine is a sign of dehydration.
rest: Total rest means no work, no heavy chores, and no stress. Give your body 48 hours of genuine quiet to kickstart healing.
pollen: Check local pollen counts. Keep windows closed on high count days and shower immediately after being outdoors.
dust: Use a damp cloth for dusting to avoid scattering allergens into the air. HEPA filters are excellent for bedroom use.
dander: If you have pet allergies, keep pets out of the bedroom and use an air purifier to reduce airborne dander.
food allergy: Carry an EpiPen if you have severe food allergies. Even 'masked' ingredients in restaurant food can cause reactions.
skin irritant: Switch to fragrance-free detergents and soaps if you have a rash. Avoid scratching as it can cause secondary infection.
sugar: Excessive sugar can temporarily weaken white blood cells. Limit sweets while fighting an infection.
salt: High salt intake causes water retention and increases blood pressure. Aim for under 2300mg of sodium per day.
fiber: Fiber (25-30g daily) is essential for gut health. Add it slowly to your diet to avoid bloating and gas.
probiotics: Found in yogurt, kefir, and kimchi. They support the 'good' bacteria that comprise 70% of your immune system.
nettie pot: Use ONLY distilled or sterilized water in a nettie pot to prevent rare but dangerous sinus infections.
hot water bottle: Excellent for warming up during chills or soothing back pain. Ensure it is not too hot to avoid skin burns.
pillow: Use a firm pillow for neck support. If you have back pain, place a pillow under your knees while sleeping on your back.
room temperature: The ideal temperature for healing sleep is between 60-67°F (15-19°C). Too much heat can cause restless sleep.
light sensitivity: Migraines often require a pitch-black room. Use blackout curtains or an eye mask for deep recovery.
sounds: White noise or rainfall sounds can block out disruptive household noises and help you sink into restorative sleep.
bedtime: Consistency is key. Go to sleep at the same time every night to keep your circadian rhythm and immune system synced.
hygiene: Maintain a clean environment. Change your pillowcases every 2 days if you have a skin infection or a cold.
ventilation: Open windows for 10 minutes a day, even in winter, to flush out indoor pollutants and concentrated pathogens.
stretching: Hold stretches for 30 seconds. If you feel sharp pain, stop immediately. Focus on the hamstrings and lower back.
fruit: Berries and kiwis are superfoods for recovery. They are low in sugar and high in antioxidants and Vitamin C.
vegetables: Cruciferous vegetables like broccoli contain sulforaphane, which helps detoxify your cells and supports raw energy.
sodium: Look for 'low sodium' labels on canned goods. Rinse canned beans to remove up to 40% of the preserved salt.
potassium: Found in bananas and potatoes. It helps balance sodium and supports healthy heart and muscle function.
